title: With Due Respect (Vol. 4) -- Ch. 4: Should Libel be Decriminalized?
primary_topics: Chapter 4 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 4) -- CJP's April 27, 2008 Inquirer column on the pending bills to decriminalize libel (either abolishing it as a crime or removing imprisonment in favor of fines)

Retired Justice Vicente Mendoza's case against outright decriminalization -- that free speech can be abused 'to destroy the reputation... of others,' and 'the right to one's honor is oftentimes more valuable than... property' -- balanced against the reality that 'the powerful and the rich' also abuse libel suits to harass journalists

Mendoza's alternative: distinguish 'political' from 'private' libel, treating criticism of public officials as 'privileged' (presumed good faith) so they can be convicted only on proof of 'actual malice' -- consistent with Vasquez v. Court of Appeals (1999), which made truth a complete defense for criticism of officials

How the Court had already protected the press without waiting for Congress -- via Administrative Circular 08-2008's 'rule of preference' for fines over imprisonment, applied in Fermin v. People (2008) to impose only a P6,000 fine in lieu of jail
sub_topics: The bills: several measures pending in Congress would either abolish libel as a crime or delete imprisonment as a sanction and 'retain fine as the only penalty'

Mendoza's objection: in Senate testimony, retired Justice Vicente Mendoza opposed decriminalization, noting that free speech 'can and has been used as a calumny... to destroy the reputation' of others, and that 'the right to one's honor is oftentimes more valuable than the right to property,' since a reputation 'tattered by scurrilous defamation is more difficult to restore than stolen goods'
The Revised Penal Code: its provisions (Articles 353-362) penalize libel, slander and 'intriguing against honor' to protect the reputation of 'peace-loving citizens'

The countervailing abuse: 'the powerful and the rich can likewise abuse their right to prosecute,' choosing 'inconvenient venues' and hiring 'odious lawyers who heckle and harass penniless defendants' -- and, worse, journalists 'become victims of unexplained disappearances and extralegal killings'

Mendoza's middle way: distinguish 'political' libel (defamation of public officials or public figures for their official duties or showbiz careers) from 'private' libel -- treating criticism of public officials as 'privileged' and presumed made 'in good faith,' so the writer is guilty only if the prosecution proves 'actual malice' (the imputation is false and the defendant knew it was false), while keeping the existing burden on defendants in private-individual cases

The Senate reaction: Sen. Richard Gordon (chair of the Committee on Constitutional Amendments) supported the distinction, while Sens. Juan Ponce Enrile and Joker Arroyo voiced 'reservations against... decriminalization,' saying 'the law is already lenient on media'

The jurisprudence: the proposal aligns with Vasquez v. Court of Appeals (September 15, 1999), which held truth a complete defense and ruled that for statements on official conduct 'no liability can attach... unless the public official... proves... actual malice' -- reversing old jurisprudence that made the accused prove absence of malice

The Court's head start: Administrative Circular 08-2008 (January 25, 2008) declared an 'emergent rule of preference for the imposition of fine only rather than imprisonment in libel cases,' a preference applied in Fermin v. People (March 28, 2008), where the Court (through Justice Nachura) fined 'Gossip Tabloid' publisher Cristy Fermin only P6,000 'in lieu of imprisonment' for libel against Annabelle Rama and Eddie Gutierrez -- part of the judiciary's care to protect news professionals from 'harassment suits'

stances.claim: Libel need not be decriminalized to protect press freedom: the better path is Mendoza's distinction between 'political' and 'private' libel, treating criticism of public officials as 'privileged' and punishable only on proof of 'actual malice,' while preserving ordinary protection for private individuals' reputations.
stances.rhetorical_move: third-way endorsement: rejecting the binary of crime-or-no-crime in favor of a targeted reform
stances.confidence: presented approvingly as the sounder option

stances.claim: Reputation deserves real protection -- 'the right to one's honor is oftentimes more valuable than the right to property' -- yet the law is also abused by 'the powerful and the rich' to harass journalists with inconvenient venues and 'odious lawyers,' so reform must protect both honor and the press.
stances.rhetorical_move: two-sided balancing: acknowledging abuse on both sides to justify a calibrated rather than blunt reform

stances.claim: Even without congressional action, the Court has already shielded journalists -- making truth a complete defense for criticism of officials (Vasquez) and preferring fines over jail (Administrative Circular 08-2008, applied in Fermin) -- 'to encourage fair criticism especially of public officials.'
stances.rhetorical_move: the-courts-acted-first: showing jurisprudence and circulars have moved ahead of the legislature
stances.confidence: asserted with case and circular support

notable_anecdotes: Honor over property: CJP relays Mendoza's argument that a reputation 'tattered by scurrilous defamation is more difficult to restore than stolen goods or money.'

Harassment by the powerful: he notes that wealthy plaintiffs pick 'inconvenient venues' and hire 'odious lawyers who heckle and harass penniless defendants' -- and that some journalists face 'disappearances and extralegal killings.'
Truth as a defense: he ties the proposal to Vasquez v. Court of Appeals, which made truth a complete defense and required proof of 'actual malice' for criticism of officials.
The P6,000 fine: he cites Fermin v. People, where the Court fined 'Gossip Tabloid' publisher Cristy Fermin only P6,000 'in lieu of imprisonment,' as the new preference in action.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 4 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 4), CJP's April 27, 2008 Inquirer column, weighs the pending bills to decriminalize libel -- either abolishing it as a crime or replacing imprisonment with fines. He presents retired Justice Vicente Mendoza's Senate testimony against outright decriminalization: free speech 'can and has been used as a calumny... to destroy the reputation' of others, and 'the right to one's honor is oftentimes more valuable than the right to property,' since a defamed reputation is 'more difficult to restore than stolen goods.' Yet CJP balances this against abuse from the other side -- 'the powerful and the rich' who file libel suits in 'inconvenient venues' with 'odious lawyers' to harass penniless journalists, some of whom suffer 'disappearances and extralegal killings.' Mendoza's middle way, which CJP favors, is to distinguish 'political' from 'private' libel: criticism of public officials for their official conduct would be 'privileged' and presumed in good faith, so a writer could be convicted only on proof of 'actual malice' (the imputation false and known to be false), while ordinary protection would remain for private individuals. The Senate was split -- Sen. Gordon backed the distinction; Sens. Enrile and Joker Arroyo had 'reservations' since 'the law is already lenient on media.' The proposal, CJP notes, tracks Vasquez v. Court of Appeals (1999), which made truth a complete defense and required proof of 'actual malice' for statements on official conduct, reversing older jurisprudence. And even before Congress acts, the Court had already moved: Administrative Circular 08-2008 declared a 'rule of preference for... fine only rather than imprisonment,' applied in Fermin v. People (2008), where Justice Nachura's ruling fined 'Gossip Tabloid' publisher Cristy Fermin just P6,000 'in lieu of imprisonment' for libel against Annabelle Rama and Eddie Gutierrez -- part of the judiciary's care, CJP writes, to 'encourage fair criticism especially of public officials, and to protect journalists from harassment.'
